opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think memory is really one of the underappreciated pieces of the story when people talk about AI hardware. Everyone focuses on FLOPs, but for a lot of what's happening now, especially post-training, the bottleneck is really about how much model state you can hold and how quickly you can get to it.

With our reconfigurable dataflow architecture, we made a deliberate decision early on to build a memory hierarchy with three tiers. You've got the on-chip SRAM distributed across the fabric, which is what makes the dataflow execution efficient, since you can keep intermediate results on chip and avoid round trips to memory. Then you've got high-bandwidth memory, and then a large tier of DDR capacity attached to each socket. That last tier gives you a very large memory footprint per system compared to a GPU-based design, where you're constrained by the HBM on each device.

Why does that matter for post-training? Think about what people are doing: fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from feedback, distillation, building lots of specialized variants of a base model. In many of these workflows you need multiple models resident at once. In RL-style post-training you might have a policy model, a reference model, a reward model, and you're doing generation as part of the training loop. On a GPU cluster you end up sharding all of that across many devices, and you pay a big price in communication and in the complexity of orchestrating it.

When you have a large memory capacity, you can keep those models close together on a much smaller number of chips. You can also keep many fine-tuned checkpoints or experts available and switch between them quickly, which is the idea behind what we've called a composition of experts. Instead of one monolithic model, you have lots of specialized models that you can hot-swap in milliseconds, because they're sitting in memory rather than being loaded from storage.

So the combination is really the point: dataflow gives you efficient execution of the operators, and the memory hierarchy gives you capacity to keep the whole working set of the post-training process resident. That means you can iterate faster, use fewer systems, and make it practical for enterprises to customize models on their own data rather than having to rely on a single giant general-purpose model.

r001.rationale: The response describes memory capacity and access as key post-training bottlenecks. It does not identify a shift from memory access during inference to computation during training.

r002.rationale: It describes a DDR capacity tier beyond HBM and says the larger memory footprint lets post-training models stay resident together, implying DDR can hold some of the working set instead of requiring it all to fit in HBM.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. So the way I think about it is that post-training is really where the memory pressure shows up. In pre-training you've got one big model and a fairly regular pattern: you shard it, you run through tokens, and the working set is predictable. Post-training is messier. If you look at RLHF or any of the reinforcement-learning-from-verifiable-rewards loops people are running now, you've got a policy model, a reference model, often a reward model, maybe a critic, plus the rollouts and the KV cache for generation, all of which want to be resident at the same time. On a GPU-based system, where you're bounded by the HBM you can put on each device, that forces you to either spread across a very large number of chips, with all the interconnect overhead that implies, or to constantly swap models in and out, which kills your utilization.

What we did with the SambaNova architecture is build a three-tier memory system. There's on-chip SRAM, which is very fast but small, then HBM, and then a large pool of DDR memory attached directly to the chips, on the order of terabytes per node. So you can hold multiple full-size models, or several variants of the same model, close to the compute and switch between them in microseconds rather than seconds. That means the policy and the reference and the reward model can all live on the same system, and the generation phase and the training phase don't have to fight over the same scarce HBM.

The other piece is that the dataflow execution model lets us fuse the whole graph of a forward pass, or a forward-and-backward pass, into a single pipelined computation on the chip. So the compiler sees the whole thing and streams data through the stages, instead of launching kernels one at a time and going back to memory in between. When you combine that with the large memory tier, you get high utilization even on the generation-heavy parts of post-training, which is exactly where GPUs tend to be inefficient because inference and training have such different compute-to-memory ratios.

So in practice, large memory is what lets us treat post-training as one integrated workload on one system, rather than stitching together an inference cluster and a training cluster and shuttling weights between them. And as we move toward things like agentic loops and test-time compute, where the model is generating a lot before you ever compute a gradient, I think that gap only gets wider.

r001.rationale: The response says inference and training have different compute-to-memory ratios and describes memory pressure during post-training, but it does not identify a shift from memory access as the inference bottleneck to computation as the training bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes DDR memory as a large tier that can hold multiple full-size models near the compute, and says generation and training need not compete for scarce HBM.

astra-6.text:
Large memory is important because post-training involves more than just running a model forward. You need to hold the model weights, the activations, gradients, and potentially optimizer state. And depending on the approach, you may have multiple models involved, so the memory requirements can grow quite substantially.

The way I think about it is that you need both capacity and fast access to the data you’re actively computing on. Our architecture combines a large memory capacity with on-chip memory and a programmable dataflow that lets us move data through the computation efficiently. That gives us flexibility in how we map these workloads, while keeping the compute resources busy.

So the benefit isn’t simply that you can fit a larger model. It’s that you can work with that model without having to spread everything across a large number of devices just to get enough memory. That can reduce the communication overhead and make adapting a model to a particular task much more practical.

r001.rationale: The response discusses memory needs and keeping compute resources busy, but does not identify a shift from memory access as the inference bottleneck to computation as the training bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention DDR or HBM, or state that training data can be held in DDR instead of residing entirely in HBM.

sol-6.1.text:
Large memory is really important because post-training is about more than just holding the model weights. When you’re fine-tuning, you also have activations, gradients, and optimizer state, and those can require substantially more memory than inference alone.

If you can keep that working set close to the compute, you avoid a lot of the communication and data movement that otherwise become bottlenecks. And that fits with our dataflow approach: organizing the computation and the memory together so that the compute units stay busy.

It also gives you flexibility. You can work with larger models, longer sequences, or different training strategies without having to partition everything across more devices simply to get enough memory. The key is that capacity and bandwidth have to work together—having a lot of memory is useful when the architecture can feed the computation efficiently.

r001.rationale: It says post-training has a large working set and that data movement can bottleneck performance, but it does not state that the bottleneck shifts from memory access during inference to computation during training.

r002.rationale: It discusses memory capacity generally but does not mention DDR or say training data can reside in DDR instead of all being held in HBM.
